query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Near-equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability at high operating temperatures because their high configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatches create lattice strain fields that kinetically impede atomic diffusion and elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized multi-element nanoparticles with near-equiatomic composition, displaying a single-phase random solid-solution atomic distribution (e.g., mixtures including low contents of noble metals).
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles that are nearly equiatomic but differ in their atomic size mismatch by intentionally varying elemental combinations. Then, subject both sets to high-temperature exposures in inert or mildly reactive atmospheres simulating catalytic (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service conditions.
generation.conditions: Controlled high-temperature exposure in an environment that mimics catalytic or thermoelectric service regimes, with careful control of atmosphere and consistent particle size distributions.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale lattice strain induced by differences in atomic radii and the resulting chemical disorder. This mediator influences the rate of elemental diffusion and phase separation under thermal exposure.
generation.mechanism: In nanoparticles with pronounced atomic-size mismatch, the resultant lattice strain and high configurational entropy create kinetic barriers to atomic rearrangement. This suppresses segregation and phase separation at elevated temperatures. Conversely, nanoparticles with minimal size mismatch will have lower lattice strain and may allow easier atomic diffusion, leading to earlier onset of phase instability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature conditions, nanoparticles exhibiting greater atomic-size mismatch should better preserve their single-phase solid-solution structure and uniform elemental distribution compared to those with minimal mismatch, which are expected to show signs of elemental segregation or phase separation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with minimal atomic-size mismatch (i.e., elemental combinations with more similar atomic radii) are expected to have lower lattice strain and thus a lower resistance to thermally induced segregation.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is expected to hold as long as the operating temperature does not exceed the fundamental thermodynamic stability limit of the solid solution or if the mixing enthalpy between the elements remains moderately favorable. Extreme temperatures or very unfavorable elemental interactions may override the kinetic stabilization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold of atomic-size mismatch required for significant stabilization, as well as the exact temperature limits, remain uncertain and require experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one with intentionally enhanced atomic-size mismatch and one with minimized mismatch. Expose both sets to high-temperature environments representative of catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions. Use in-situ structural and compositional analysis techniques to monitor the evolution of phase structure and elemental distribution over time.
measurements: High-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect phase changes or the onset of segregation
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for nanoscale compositional mapping
Catalytic activity tests and thermoelectric property measurements (e.g., conductivity, Seebeck coefficient) to correlate performance with structural stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with higher atomic-size mismatch do not exhibit improved resistance to phase separation (i.e., if both sets show similar or no improvement in maintaining single-phase structure and uniform elemental distribution), then the hypothesis that lattice strain from atomic-size mismatch stabilizes the high-temperature structure is falsified.
